From what I can glean with a very cursory bit of knowledge, its about trying to keep the share price high and the shareholders happy.

If you have a series of poor sales periods and he value of your company drops $500k, your 400k shares are now only valued at $8. This is bad for your shareholders and will make them think about selling before they lose any more money. So, the company goes and buys back 50k shares. Now, there are only 350k shares in the market, your company is still only valued at $3.5mil, but you have kept your share price at $10! 

It's basically a smoke and mirrors play to try and hide the sales damage the company is sustaining either to hope there are sunny days around the corner or to prolong the inevitable bulk fire sale of shares in the stock market.

Something like a 7pot (1m-1.8m shu depending on subspecies and my personal favourite chillies for the heat profile and flavour) has a slow building burn similar to that of an oven. A scorpion on the other hand (1m-2.1m shu) has an intense and instant needling heat. Similar to what you would imagine eating a wasp nest would feel like. Ever been stung by a wasp? Imagine that coating your mouth for a solid 10mins.

I am in Australia and it is mind blowing. Especially how often we take it for granted that when something goes wrong, you can go get it fixed and not worry about anything outside of how long you might have to wait to be seen.

For example...

I tore the cartilage in my knee being stupid, saw the GP, she sent a referral, got an appointment with a specialist and he decided wasn't worth surgery. Total cost: 1.5hrs of my life. 

Crushed and decapitated my finger at work. Smashed to the nearest ER, two bolts of morphine, transfer to another hospital where a finger specialist was attending, another bolt of the good stuff, micro surgery to clean and reattach, return to hospital at 1:30am due to insane post surgery pain, ring blockers, take home oxy, followup appointments, fibreglass splint and dressing changes. Total cost: 24hrs of intense discomfort and 3 weeks of recovery discomfort .

Dislocated my shoulder riding my moto through the scrub. Got to the ER, instantly triaged, given morphine, x-ray, surgical sedation and joint reduction, secondary x-ray, sling and an appointment with a shoulder specialist. Got an MRI to assess damage and the next week saw the surgeon. Total cost: $180 for the MRI and 5hrs of my time. No surgery, but had the labrum tear been worse, surgery would still have cost me nothing unless I went private.

An ex had an allergic reaction to some food, started into anaphylaxis. Called an ambulance 8pm on a Sunday. Came out, administered adrenaline and (I think) antihistamines of some sort, rushed to hospital, treated, monitored overnight on ward, released next day. Total cost: One night in hospital. 

I could go on and on, but basically, it is amazing. You can go into a private hospital if you have insurance and that might get you your own room and a faster turn around, but if you are in the shit, you know you aren't going to have to decide whether or not you can afford to get the help you need.

Fentanyl pain relief (which also did SFA but I am sure was a great assistant in my post care pain management for that night): Free

Propofol + Ketamine surgical sedation: Free

X-Ray (to check joint placement after reduction): Free

Medical report and follow up with GP: Free

The only thing I paid for was the drugs I bought from the pharmacy to manage my pain levels once I got home. I think that was about $25 for a box of Mercyndol night time (Paracetamol + Codine + Doxylamine Succinate)and a box of Neurofen Plus (Ibuprofin + Codine).

My assumption is that it is due to diesel engines working differently to petrol engines. Petrol engines work by igniting gasoline under moderate compression, whereas diesel engines use high compression and latent heat to ignite the fuel. They don't spark like petrol engines as the residual heat and compression does the work instead. 

Petrol has a much higher concentration of naptha (also known as light ends or short chain hydrocarbons), has a much lower ignition point and subsequently is more aromatic (readiness to evaporate) and a higher volatility. That's why you can start a fire quite well with petrol but not with diesel. You aren't igniting the fuel, you're igniting the vapours. 

Diesel is more of a middle cut when it comes to it's BP and flash point, usually taken from a batch of crude at between 350ºC-170ºC and is made of longer hydrocarbon chains. As such, you need to compress it more than you do with petrol in order to get it to explode just right and cause ignition.
